## What's new

- **The last five commands have keys.** Everything the command line can do,
  the window can do — and it is checked rather than claimed now. `r2b ls` is
  <kbd>f</kbd>, `restore --machine` is <kbd>c</kbd>, `restore --verify` is a
  field on the restore form, `remove --purge` is <kbd>X</kbd>, and
  `schedule --repair` is <kbd>p</kbd>.

- **See what is in your bucket, from your bucket.** Press <kbd>c</kbd> on
  Folders for every backup stored, this computer's and your other computers',
  and press enter to restore one. This is what a machine that has just signed
  in needs: it has working credentials, an empty folder list, and until now
  nothing on screen naming the data that was already there.

- **What is stored, with sizes.** Press <kbd>f</kbd> on a folder for the
  objects it holds, largest first, and the total. It reads the local index,
  so it costs no operations.

- **Delete a folder's stored copy without leaving the window.** <kbd>X</kbd>
  stops backing a folder up and deletes every object stored for it. It asks
  you to type the folder's name back first, which is the same bar `--purge`
  sets on the command line.

- **Adding your first folder offers to keep backing it up.** The command has
  always ended by asking; the window said nothing, so a folder added there was
  backed up exactly once unless you went and found the Schedule mode. It is
  asked once, after the first backup finishes, and never when backups are
  already scheduled.

- **A prettier sign-in email.** The six-digit code arrives as a designed
  message rather than one line of plain text — and it loads nothing: no
  hosted images, no web font, no tracking pixel. It has a dark version, and
  it says the code's real lifetime rather than a number written into the copy.

## Fixed

- **Uploads were lost when the network hiccupped.** A file that hit a
  transient failure mid-upload could not be retried: the retry needs to rewind
  the file, and the progress counter wrapped around it hid the file's own
  ability to rewind. On a busy connection this failed dozens of files at once,
  each reported as a failed upload. Nothing was ever silently skipped — they
  were counted and named — but they needed another run to go up.

- **The window never showed which version it was.** The header had a slot for
  it that was never filled in.

- **The keyboard help was trimmed for a terminal you were not using.** It was
  cut at two fixed widths, so a mode with more to offer lost more of its keys
  regardless of how wide the window actually was. It is measured now, and
  <kbd>tab</kbd> and <kbd>q</kbd> survive every width.
